name: Urophagia

lead: Urophagia, usually called urine therapy, is the practice of drinking or otherwise applying one's own urine for health and cosmetic purposes. Within appearance circles, adherents connect it to clearer skin, a better complexion and general vitality, and some also massage urine onto skin or gums.

The idea has roots in folk medicine and in a 20th-century naturopathic movement. Medical organisations such as the American Cancer Society state that scientific evidence does not support the health claims made for it, and the published medical literature consists mainly of case reports of harm.

paras: Practitioners describe drinking their own midstream morning urine, sometimes over a period of days or weeks, and in some traditions applying it to the skin or gums. Some combine it with fasting. Accounts of how long until visible skin changes appear vary by individual and are anecdotal.

Urine contains concentrated waste products and salts. A 2022 case report describes severe hypernatremia with acute kidney injury in a patient who drank his own urine while ill. Medical authorities discourage the practice, particularly for people who are dehydrated or have kidney or other illnesses.

angle.text: Adherents drink their own urine or massage it into the skin in the belief that it clears blemishes and improves complexion. Topical use is sometimes compared to urea moisturisers, which contain synthetic urea at higher concentrations than urine does [2].

lead: Urophagia, more commonly marketed as urine therapy, urotherapy or auto-urine therapy, is the use of human urine, most often one's own, for medicinal or cosmetic purposes, including drinking it and rubbing it onto skin or gums [1][2]. In Hindu and Ayurvedic-inspired circles it is called shivambu [2].

Within appearance-oriented communities, the stated aim is better skin and a healthier-looking complexion, in line with broader claims that the practice detoxifies the body or boosts immunity. Practitioners also use urine topically on skin, a use that overlaps with the way commercial urea creams are used as moisturisers [2].

Medical and cancer-research bodies report that scientific evidence does not support the claimed benefits, and the clinical literature includes a case report of severe hypernatremia (high blood sodium) and kidney injury after a patient ingested his own urine [1][2].

paras: Urine is about 95 percent water, with the rest made up of dissolved waste products such as urea, creatinine and uric acid, along with electrolytes and trace hormones and vitamins [3]. Practitioners of urine therapy drink their own urine, sometimes fresh from the stream, and in some variants use it on the skin, scalp or gums [2].

Proponents describe it as a natural, free remedy. They point to its presence in traditional medicine and argue that the body's own fluid carries beneficial compounds, a reasoning that medical sources do not share [2][3].

Urine appears in a number of traditional medical systems and in older European remedy books, and reports state that Roman dentists used it to whiten teeth [2]. Hindu and Ayurvedic traditions refer to it as shivambu, and some modern writers cite the Damar Tantra as an ancient source [2][3].

The British naturopath John W. Armstrong popularised auto-urine therapy in the early twentieth century, prescribing it from 1918 and publishing The Water of Life in 1944 [2]. The Indian social reformer Raojibhai Manibhai Patel published Manav mootra in 1959, inspired by Armstrong. The anthropologist Joseph Alter has argued that modern Indian urine therapy resembles Armstrong's regimen more than it does classical Ayurveda or yoga [2]. Organisations promoting urine therapy exist in several countries, including a Urine Therapy Association in China that was listed as illegal by the government in 2016 [2].

Believers state that urine therapy detoxifies the body, strengthens immunity and treats conditions ranging from skin complaints to serious disease. Some alternative clinics have offered it to cancer patients [2]. For appearance, the claims focus on skin clarity and a healthy glow, and on topical use against blemishes.
The American Cancer Society states that available scientific evidence does not support claims that urine or urea in any form helps cancer patients [2].

No controlled trials of drinking urine for skin or appearance outcomes were found. The published clinical literature includes a 2022 case report of a severely debilitated patient with acute gouty arthritis who drank his own urine and developed severe hypernatremia with acute kidney injury. The authors proposed that the high urea load caused osmotic diuresis and increased free-water loss, and they described it as the first report of this cause of hypernatremia [1].

Because urine is the body's route for excreting wastes, re-ingesting it returns concentrated salts and urea. This can contribute to dehydration and electrolyte imbalance, as in the 2022 case [1][3]. Urine leaves the body through the urethra and so is no longer sterile once voided, and urine from another person can carry excreted medications [3].
Dermatology sources note that commercial urea creams work as moisturisers at high concentrations of synthetic urea, whereas urine is too dilute to act in that way [2].
